text: Otto Georg Thierack (19 April 1889 – 26 October 1946) was a German Nazi jurist and politician. Born in Wurzen in Saxony, he served in the First World War from 1914 to 1918 as a volunteer, reaching the rank of lieutenant, and suffered a facial injury; he was awarded the Iron Cross, second class. After the war, he resumed his law studies and completed them in 1920 with his Assessor (junior lawyer) examination. That same year, he was hired as a court Assessor in Saxony. On 1 August 1932, Thierack joined the Nazi Party. Following the Nazis' seizure of power in 1933, he rapidly advanced from prosecutor to President of the People's Court (Volksgerichtshof), a rise facilitated not only by his Nazi Party membership but also by his leadership of the National Socialist jurists' organization, the Rechtswahrerbund. Appointed Saxony's justice minister on 12 May 1933, Thierack was tasked with "nazifying" the region's judicial administration. After holding several mid-level judicial positions, he became vice president of the Reich Court in 1935 and, in May 1936, president of the Volksgerichtshof, which had been established in 1934. He held this position until August 1942, when he was succeeded by Roland Freisler, despite two interruptions due to service in the armed forces. On 20 August 1942, he succeeded Hans Frank as President of the Academy for German Law. On the same date, he became Reich Minister of Justice. In October 1942, he introduced the monthly Richterbriefe, which provided model judicial decisions from the Nazi perspective, with names omitted, to guide German jurisprudence. He also introduced the Vorschauen and Nachschauen ("previews" and "inspections"), requiring higher state court presidents, in cases of public interest, to discuss with the public prosecutor's office and the State Court president—whom they had to forward to responsible criminal courts—how a case would be judged before a final decision. Upon becoming Reich Minister of Justice in August 1942, Thierack streamlined the lengthy clemency procedures for death sentences. In September 1942, he classified all prisoners who were "Jews, Gypsies, Russians, Poles sentenced to over three years, Czechs, or Germans serving a sentence of over eight years" as "asocial elements" and transferred them to Reichsführer-SS Heinrich Himmler for forced labor to death. At Thierack's initiative, the execution shed at Plötzensee Prison in Berlin was equipped with eight iron hooks in December 1942 to enable the simultaneous hanging of multiple individuals (a guillotine had already existed there). Mass executions began on 7 September 1943, though some prisoners were hanged by mistake; Thierack dismissed these as errors and insisted that the hangings continue. Thierack was named to continue as Minister of Justice in Hitler's political testament. He served in the brief Goebbels cabinet but was dismissed on 5 May 1945 by Hitler's successor, Reichspräsident Karl Dönitz. After the end of World War II, the Allies arrested Thierack. Before being tried at the Nuremberg Judges' Trial, he committed suicide in Sennelager, Paderborn, by poisoning himself.
